title: Little Sisters of the Poor Saints Peter and Paul Home v. Pennsylvania (2020)
shortTitle: Little Sisters of the Poor Saints Peter and Paul Home v. Pennsylvania (2020)
summary: A final rule could satisfy the APA through the notice and comment invited in interim rules; courts could not add an open-mindedness procedural test.
notes: Justice Thomas wrote for a 7-2 Court that reversed the Third Circuit and remanded; Justice Alito concurred (joined by Gorsuch), Justice Kagan concurred in the judgment (joined by Breyer), and Justice Ginsburg dissented (joined by Sotomayor). The case was consolidated with Trump v. Pennsylvania, and the challengers were Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

sections.Parties: Pennsylvania and New Jersey challenged federal contraceptive-coverage exemptions. The Departments of Health and Human Services, Labor, and Treasury defended their rules, and the Little Sisters intervened to defend the religious exemption.
sections.Material Facts: In 2017 the Departments issued interim final rules expanding religious exemptions and establishing moral-objection exemptions to contraceptive coverage. They invoked good cause and solicited comments. While litigation proceeded, the Departments finalized the rules in 2018, responding to comments while keeping the exemptions largely intact.
sections.Procedural History: The district court enjoined the interim rules. After amended pleadings addressing the final rules, it entered another nationwide preliminary injunction; the Third Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court rejected the statutory-authority and procedural grounds relied upon below. The assigned excerpt primarily presents the notice-and-comment analysis, summarizes the statutory conclusion, and omits separate opinions and the final mandate’s wording.
sections.Issue: Did the earlier use of interim final rules invalidate the later final rules, and could a reviewing court demand evidence that the agency maintained an open mind beyond the APA’s prescribed procedures?
sections.Holding: The final rules satisfied the APA’s procedural requirements. The Court found authority under the ACA to create exemptions and considered attention to RFRA appropriate, while declining to decide whether RFRA independently authorized or compelled the exemptions. It did not need to decide whether good cause justified the 2017 interim rules.
sections.Reasoning: The interim publications supplied legal authority, detailed proposed substance, and a request for comments; their title did not deprive the public of notice. Even a naming defect would require prejudicial error, which the challengers did not show. The public received 60 days to comment, the final rules explained their basis and purpose, and publication preceded effectiveness by more than 30 days. Under Vermont Yankee and Perez, courts could not add an open-mindedness procedure to the APA’s requirements. Similarity between the interim and final texts did not itself establish procedural invalidity. The editorial note qualifies the practical lesson: the interim rules had been quickly enjoined, so commenters were not living under their operation while commenting. The decision does not settle every substantive arbitrary-and-capricious challenge to the scope of the exemptions.

topics.lrs-n-good-cause: The Court evaluated the later final rules independently of the unresolved good-cause justification for the earlier interim rules.
topics.lrs-o-section-553: The Court held that a request for comments in an interim final rule can satisfy § 553's notice requirement for the final rule.
topics.lrs-s-enabling-statute: The Court found authority for the exemptions in the ACA's grant to HRSA to define required preventive coverage.
